questions.stem: What is the sample space of a random experiment?
options: The results recorded in a simulation
The single most likely outcome
The set of all possible outcomes
The outcomes that count as a success
questions.explanation: The sample space lists every outcome that could occur, and every event is a subset of it. Recorded results are a sample drawn from it, not the sample space itself.

questions.stem: A coin is tossed and a six-sided die is rolled. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
questions.explanation: Each of the 2 coin results can pair with each of the 6 die results, giving 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes. Adding instead gives 8, which undercounts the pairs.

questions.stem: A random variable is best described as:
options: the number of times a random experiment is repeated
the probability that a random event will occur
a rule giving a number to each outcome of a random experiment
a variable whose value is chosen by the experimenter
questions.explanation: For two coin tosses, X = the number of heads gives HH the value 2, HT and TH the value 1, and TT the value 0. A random variable is a number attached to outcomes, not a probability.

questions.stem: The outcomes of an experiment are a, b, c and d, with probabilities 0.1, 0.3, 0.4 and p. What is the value of p?
questions.explanation: The probabilities over a sample space must add to 1, so p = 1 − (0.1 + 0.3 + 0.4) = 0.2. The value 0.25 assumes all four outcomes are equally likely.

questions.stem: Which list could be the probabilities of the three outcomes of an experiment?
questions.explanation: Probabilities must be non-negative and must add to 1. The list 0.6, 0.5, −0.1 adds to 1 but contains a negative value, and the other two lists add to 1.2 and 0.75.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled. Which event is a compound event?
options: Rolling an even number
Rolling a number greater than 5
Rolling a 4
Rolling a 1
questions.explanation: A compound event contains more than one outcome; rolling an even number is 2, 4 or 6. Rolling a number greater than 5 sounds broader but contains only the outcome 6, so it is elementary.

questions.stem: Pr(A) = 0.35. What is Pr(A′), the probability that A does not occur?
questions.explanation: A and its complement A′ together make up the whole sample space, so Pr(A′) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65. A value of 1.35 adds instead of subtracting, and no probability can exceed 1.

questions.stem: Two coins are tossed and X is the number of heads. What is Pr(X = 1)?
questions.explanation: The four equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT, and two of them have exactly one head, so Pr(X = 1) = 2/4 = 1/2. The value 1/3 treats the three values 0, 1 and 2 as equally likely, which they are not.

questions.stem: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 7?
questions.explanation: A 6 × 6 grid has 36 equally likely outcomes, and six of them sum to 7: (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2), (6, 1). The answer 1/11 treats the eleven possible sums as equally likely.

questions.stem: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the product of the numbers is even?
questions.explanation: The product is odd only when both numbers are odd, with probability 3/6 × 3/6 = 1/4, so Pr(even) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The answer 1/4 is the probability of an odd product.

questions.stem: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the two numbers differ by 2?
questions.explanation: The pairs are (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 6) and the same four reversed, giving 8 of the 36 outcomes, so 8/36 = 2/9. Counting each pair only once gives 1/9.

questions.stem: The larger of the two numbers shown on two fair dice is recorded. What is the probability that it is 2?
questions.explanation: The outcomes with largest number 2 are (1, 2), (2, 1) and (2, 2), which is 3 of 36, or 1/12. Leaving out (2, 2) gives 2/36 = 1/18.

questions.stem: Spinner A shows 1, 2 or 3 and spinner B shows 1 or 2, each with equally likely outcomes. Both are spun. What is the probability that the sum is 3?
questions.explanation: The 3 × 2 = 6 outcomes are equally likely, and two of them, (1, 2) and (2, 1), sum to 3, giving 2/6 = 1/3. The answer 1/4 treats the four possible sums 2 to 5 as equally likely.

questions.stem: In a class of 30, 18 students play sport, 12 play music and 5 do both. How many students do neither?
questions.explanation: Students in at least one group: 18 + 12 − 5 = 25, because the 5 in both were counted twice. So 30 − 25 = 5 do neither. Forgetting the overlap gives 30 in at least one group and 0 left over.

questions.stem: In a group of 40, 25 like tea, 20 like coffee and 8 like neither. One person is chosen at random. What is the probability they like both?
questions.explanation: 32 people like at least one, so the overlap is 25 + 20 − 32 = 13 and the probability is 13/40. The value 1/5 is 8/40, the probability of liking neither.

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed three times. What is the probability of at least one head?
questions.explanation: The only outcome with no head is TTT, with probability 1/8, so Pr(at least one head) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. The value 3/8 is the probability of exactly one head.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled four times. What is the probability of at least one six?
questions.explanation: Pr(no six in four rolls) = (5/6)⁴ = 625/1296, so Pr(at least one six) = 1 − 625/1296 = 671/1296, about 0.52. Adding 1/6 four times to get 2/3 counts outcomes with several sixes more than once.

questions.stem: A spinner is spun 200 times and lands on red 46 times. What is the estimate of Pr(red) from these results?
questions.explanation: The relative frequency is 46/200 = 0.23. The value 0.46 divides by 100 instead of 200, and 0.77 is the estimate for not red.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled 60 times. How many fives would you expect?
questions.explanation: Expected number = number of trials × probability = 60 × 1/6 = 10. The actual count will vary from one set of 60 rolls to another.

questions.stem: A random number generator gives the digits 0 to 9 with equal probability. Which rule simulates an event with probability 0.3?
options: The digits 0, 1, 2 and 3 represent the event
The digit 3 alone represents the event
The digits 3 and 0 represent the event
The digits 0, 1 and 2 represent the event
questions.explanation: Each digit has probability 0.1, so three digits give 0.3. Using 0 to 3 is four digits, which is 0.4, a common counting slip.

questions.stem: Two students each toss a fair coin 20 times. One gets 13 heads and the other gets 8. What is the best conclusion?
options: Results vary between samples, and both fit a fair coin
The first coin must be biased towards heads
The second coin must be biased towards tails
At least one student tossed the coin incorrectly
questions.explanation: With only 20 tosses, counts some way from 10 are common for a fair coin, so neither result is evidence of bias. Variation between samples is expected and shrinks, as a proportion, in larger samples.

questions.stem: As the number of trials in a simulation increases, the proportion of successes:
options: alternates evenly between successes and failures
tends to settle closer to the true probability
always equals the true probability after 100 trials
becomes more and more variable from trial to trial
questions.explanation: Larger samples give relative frequencies that are less variable and cluster around the true probability. No number of trials guarantees an exact match.

questions.stem: A café offers 4 mains and 3 desserts. How many different meals of one main and one dessert are there?
questions.explanation: By the multiplication principle, each of the 4 mains can go with each of the 3 desserts: 4 × 3 = 12. Adding to get 7 counts the choice of a single dish, not a pair.

questions.stem: A student chooses one elective, either from 5 arts subjects or from 4 technology subjects. How many choices are there?
questions.explanation: The choices are alternatives that do not overlap, so by the addition principle there are 5 + 4 = 9. Multiplying to get 20 would count choosing one of each.

questions.stem: In how many ways can 5 people line up in a row?
questions.explanation: There are 5 choices for the first place, 4 for the second, and so on: 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120. The answer 3125 = 5⁵ allows the same person to stand in more than one place.

questions.stem: How many 4-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1 to 6 if no digit is repeated?
questions.explanation: There are 6 choices for the first digit, then 5, 4 and 3: 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 = 360. The answer 1296 = 6⁴ allows repeated digits, and 15 counts selections without order.

questions.stem: A number plate has 3 letters followed by 3 digits, and repetition is allowed. How many plates are possible?
questions.explanation: With repetition, each letter has 26 choices and each digit has 10: 26³ × 10³ = 17 576 × 1000 = 17 576 000. The figure 11 232 000 is 26 × 25 × 24 × 10 × 9 × 8, the count with no repetition.

questions.stem: How many 3-digit even numbers can be made from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 if no digit is repeated?
questions.explanation: Fill the restricted place first: the last digit must be 2 or 4 (2 ways), then the first digit has 4 choices and the middle has 3. So 2 × 4 × 3 = 24. The answer 60 ignores the even condition.

questions.stem: Four people, including Ana and Ben, sit in a row in random order. What is the probability that Ana and Ben sit next to each other?
questions.explanation: There are 4! = 24 orders in all. Treat Ana and Ben as one block: 3! = 6 orders of the block and the others, times 2 for the order within the block, gives 12. So 12/24 = 1/2. Forgetting the factor of 2 gives 1/4.

questions.stem: In counting, what is a combination?
options: A selection in which order does not matter
An arrangement in which order matters
A selection in which items may be repeated
A list of every outcome of an experiment
questions.explanation: A combination counts which items are chosen, so choosing A then B is the same selection as B then A. When order matters the count is of arrangements, which is larger.

questions.stem: Evaluate ⁵C₂.
questions.explanation: ⁵C₂ = 5!/(2! × 3!) = (5 × 4)/2 = 10. The value 20 = 5 × 4 counts ordered pairs, so it counts each selection twice.

questions.stem: In how many ways can a committee of 3 be chosen from 8 people?
questions.explanation: The order of choosing does not matter, so the count is ⁸C₃ = (8 × 7 × 6)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 56. The value 336 = 8 × 7 × 6 counts ordered choices and has not been divided by 3! = 6.

questions.stem: Ten people meet and each pair shakes hands once. How many handshakes are there?
questions.explanation: Each handshake is a selection of 2 people, so the count is ¹⁰C₂ = (10 × 9)/2 = 45. The value 90 = 10 × 9 counts every handshake twice, once from each person.

questions.stem: Why is ¹⁰C₃ equal to ¹⁰C₇?
options: Order does not matter, so 3 and 7 swap freely
Every number in Pascal’s triangle appears twice
Choosing 3 items to take leaves 7 items behind
Both are equal to 10 × 3 × 7 divided by 2
questions.explanation: Each selection of 3 items to include matches exactly one selection of 7 to leave out, so the counts are equal; in general, choosing r from n matches choosing n − r. The symmetry of Pascal's triangle is a consequence of this fact, not its reason, and not every number in it appears exactly twice.

questions.stem: Which expression is equal to ⁶C₂?
options: ⁶C₁ + ⁶C₃
⁵C₁ + ⁵C₂
⁵C₂ + ⁵C₃
⁵C₁ × ⁵C₂
questions.explanation: Pascal's rule gives ⁶C₂ = ⁵C₁ + ⁵C₂ = 5 + 10 = 15: each pair from 6 items either includes a particular item (5 ways) or does not (10 ways). The sum ⁵C₂ + ⁵C₃ is 20, which is ⁶C₃.

questions.stem: A lottery draws 3 different numbers from 1 to 10, and order does not matter. What is the probability that one ticket matches all three?
questions.explanation: There are ¹⁰C₃ = 120 equally likely selections, and one ticket matches exactly one of them. The value 1/720 counts ordered draws, which would only apply if the order had to match.

questions.stem: A team of 3 is chosen from 4 Year 11 and 5 Year 12 students. How many teams have exactly 2 Year 12 students?
questions.explanation: Choose the two Year 12 students in ⁵C₂ = 10 ways and the one Year 11 student in ⁴C₁ = 4 ways, then multiply: 10 × 4 = 40. Adding to get 14 treats the two choices as alternatives, and 84 = ⁹C₃ ignores the condition.

questions.stem: From 6 boys and 4 girls, a group of 3 is chosen. How many groups contain at least one girl?
questions.explanation: Count the complement: all groups ¹⁰C₃ = 120, minus the all-boy groups ⁶C₃ = 20, gives 100. Choosing one girl first and then any 2 of the other 9 gives 4 × 36 = 144, which counts groups with two or more girls more than once.

questions.stem: Two cards are drawn at random, without replacement, from a standard 52-card pack. What is the probability that both are hearts?
questions.explanation: Pr = ¹³C₂/⁵²C₂ = 78/1326 = 1/17. The value 1/16 = 1/4 × 1/4 treats the draws as independent, as if the first card were replaced, and 4/17 = 12/51 is the chance the second card is a heart given the first one was.

questions.stem: A pizza can have any selection of 5 available toppings, including no toppings. How many different pizzas are possible?
questions.explanation: Each topping is either on or off, so by the multiplication principle there are 2⁵ = 32 selections; equivalently ⁵C₀ + ⁵C₁ + … + ⁵C₅ = 32. The answer 31 leaves out the plain pizza, which the question includes.
